GETTING STARTED

Max Drawdown Types
×

The Max Drawdown is one of the most important risk parameters in futures trading and plays a major role in how Purdia Capital accounts operate. Different account types may utilize different drawdown models, and understanding how each one behaves is critical before trading.

The three primary drawdown models used throughout the funding process are:

Intraday Trailing Drawdown
End of Day (EOD) Trailing Drawdown
Static Drawdown

Each model calculates risk differently and can significantly affect trading behavior, position management, and account survivability.

It is also important to understand that all drawdown limits are active at all times while trading. Regardless of drawdown type, accounts may not fall below their minimum balance threshold at any point during trading.

An End of Day (EOD) trailing drawdown does not mean traders are permitted to trade below the drawdown threshold intraday and recover later before the end of the session. If the account balance falls below the drawdown threshold at any time, the account fails immediately.

The distinction between drawdown types is how and when the drawdown threshold itself moves — not when the rule is enforced.

Intraday Trailing Drawdown

An intraday trailing drawdown continuously updates throughout the trading day as unrealized profits increase.

This means:

Open trade profits can move the drawdown threshold higher
The drawdown follows account highs intraday
The threshold can increase even if profits are not realized

Because of this behavior, traders can permanently lose available drawdown during open positions if unrealized profits later reverse.

Example:

Starting balance: $100,000
Max drawdown: $3,000
Initial threshold: $97,000

If an open trade pushes the account to $102,000 unrealized:

The trailing threshold moves to $99,000

If the trade then reverses and the account drops below $99,000, the account fails — even if no profits were ever realized.

Intraday trailing drawdowns are generally stricter and require tighter intraday risk management.

End of Day (EOD) Trailing Drawdown

An End of Day trailing drawdown updates only after the trading session closes.

Unlike intraday trailing:

Unrealized profits during open trades do not move the threshold intraday
The drawdown level updates using the account balance at the end of the trading day
Traders retain their available intraday drawdown throughout the session

However, the drawdown threshold itself is still enforced at all times while trading.

Example:

Starting balance: $100,000
Max drawdown: $3,000
Initial threshold: $97,000

If the account rises to $102,000 during the day but closes at $101,000:

The trailing threshold updates after the session closes to $98,000

The account may not fall below the active threshold during trading at any point.

EOD trailing drawdowns generally provide traders with more flexibility during intraday price fluctuations because unrealized gains do not immediately tighten the drawdown threshold.

Static Drawdown

A static max drawdown does not trail upward as the account balance increases.

The minimum balance threshold remains fixed unless otherwise adjusted by payouts or account-specific rules.

Example:

Starting balance: $100,000
Static drawdown: $3,000
Minimum threshold: $97,000

If the account grows to $105,000:

The minimum threshold remains $97,000

Unlike trailing drawdowns, traders retain the same maximum loss threshold regardless of account growth.

Static drawdown models are commonly used in Live Funded Accounts because they provide a more stable and predictable risk environment once traders have progressed beyond the earlier funding stages.

RULES & RISK MANAGEMENT

Trading Days & Profitable Days
×

Trading Days and Profitable Days are tracked using calendar days based on US Eastern Time (ET), from midnight to midnight ET. This is separate from the futures market trading session schedule, which can sometimes create confusion when reviewing trades in Tradovate or other futures platforms.

How Trading Days Work

Some account types at Purdia Capital require a minimum number of Trading Days, Profitable Days, or both before advancing to the next stage.

For these calculations, Purdia Capital uses calendar days based on the US Eastern Time (ET) timezone. A Trading Day is any calendar day in which at least one trade is executed between 12:00 AM ET and 11:59:59 PM ET. Specifically, when the trade is closed is the time that counts.

This is especially important for traders outside the United States, as overnight futures trading in their local timezone may cross midnight ET and therefore count toward two separate Trading Days or Profitable Days under Purdia Capital’s rules.

A Profitable Day is any calendar day that meets the required profit threshold for that specific account type within that same midnight-to-midnight ET window.

This is important because futures markets themselves do not operate on normal calendar-day schedules.

Futures Trading Sessions vs Calendar Days

Most futures products trade in sessions that span across two different calendar dates. For example, many futures markets reopen at 6:00 PM ET and continue trading overnight into the following day. Because of this, Tradovate and many other futures platforms often group trades according to the futures trading session rather than according to calendar days.

This can create situations where trades that appear together inside a single Tradovate session may actually count as two different Trading Days or Profitable Days under Purdia Capital’s rules.

For example, assume a trader places one trade at 8:00 PM ET and another trade at 10:00 AM ET the following morning. Tradovate may display both trades under the same futures session. However, under Purdia Capital’s Trading Day rules, the 8:00 PM trade belongs to one calendar day, while the 10:00 AM trade belongs to the next calendar day because midnight ET occurred between them.

This can affect Trading Day counts, Profitable Day counts, and daily profit calculations.

Daily Loss Limits vs Trading Days

Another common source of confusion is that some other account risk parameters — such as Daily Loss Limits (DLLs) — follow the futures trading session schedule rather than calendar days. As a result, a DLL reset may occur at a different time than the reset for Trading Days or Profitable Days.

Currently:

Trading Days and Profitable Days reset at midnight ET
DLLs reset according to the futures trading session schedule

While this structure can occasionally create confusion, it is the current operational standard used for account tracking and progression.

Final Notes

Traders should pay close attention to overnight trading activity, especially around midnight ET, since trades placed during overnight futures sessions may count toward different Trading Days or Profitable Days than expected when reviewing the activity inside Tradovate.

If you are unsure how trades were counted toward your Trading Days or Profitable Days, contact support for clarification.
